name: StackStorm
vendor: StackStorm project (LF Projects, started by StackStorm, Inc.)

foundation.via: A series of LF Projects, LLC, handed over by Extreme Networks

summary: Event-driven automation for operations, “IFTTT for ops”: sensors turn alerts and webhooks into triggers, rules match them, and actions or YAML workflows fix the problem, with every run audited.
intro: StackStorm reacts to events. Sensors, small Python plugins, watch outside systems or receive webhooks and emit triggers, such as a monitoring alert or a Jira issue update. Rules match a trigger against criteria (`equals`, `regex`, `contains` and about two dozen other operators on fields of its payload) and start an action with parameters filled from the payload through Jinja templates. Actions are scripts or Python classes with a metadata file: run a command over SSH, call a REST API, restart a service. Workflows chain actions with branches, joins and data passed between steps, and Orquesta, StackStorm’s own YAML workflow engine, runs them. Every execution, manual or automatic, is recorded with what triggered it and what it returned.

Content ships in packs, which bundle sensors, actions, rules and workflows for one system; the StackStorm Exchange lists about 160 of them with over 6,000 actions. Action aliases expose actions to chat, so a message such as `!restart nginx on web-3` in Slack runs the same audited action (ChatOps, through a Hubot adapter). Under the hood a dozen Python services (API, auth, rules engine, scheduler, action runners, workflow engine, sensor container, timers and others) talk over RabbitMQ, keep state in MongoDB and coordinate workflow branches through Redis or ZooKeeper, with a web UI, a CLI and a REST API in front.

StackStorm 3.9.0 (October 2025) runs on Python 3.8 to 3.11 and supports MongoDB 7.0; its packages target Ubuntu 20.04 and 22.04 and RHEL or Rocky Linux 8 and 9. The next release, in development, moves to Python 3.10 to 3.12, MongoDB 8.2 and RabbitMQ 4.2, and adds packages for Ubuntu 24.04 and Rocky Linux 10. The project is maintained by volunteers from companies that run it, with most 2026 commits coming from three maintainers.
strengths: Built for auto-remediation: an alert can trigger a diagnosis and fix without a human, and every run lands in an audit trail
A large catalogue of ready integrations in the Exchange, and actions can be any script, so existing runbooks plug in as they are
The same actions run from rules, workflows, the CLI, the API and chat, with RBAC and LDAP or SSO login included in the open-source edition
Self-hosted and Apache 2.0, with no paid tier holding features back
limits: Many moving parts: RabbitMQ, MongoDB, Redis and NGINX plus about a dozen services; the docs suggest four cores and more than 16 GB of RAM for production
The Kubernetes Helm chart for high availability is still labelled beta and starts more than 30 pods by default
Slow releases from a small volunteer team: 3.8.1 in December 2023, then 3.9.0 in October 2025, and packages for Ubuntu 24.04 are not released yet

Workflows are YAML with YAQL or Jinja expressions rather than code, so complex logic ends up in Python actions, and long-running business processes fit a durable-execution engine such as Temporal better

story: Evan Powell and Dmitri Zimine founded StackStorm in 2013 to automate the operational chores that DevOps teams still did by hand: noticing an event, working out what it meant and running the fix. The company came out of stealth in May 2014 and released its platform as open source, pitched as “IFTTT for ops” for auto-remediation, incident response and deployments.

Brocade bought the eight-person company in March 2016 to bring the same automation to networking, and sold a commercial edition as Brocade Workflow Composer. When Extreme Networks bought Brocade’s data-centre networking business in October 2017, StackStorm went with it and the product became Extreme Workflow Composer.

On 7 October 2019 Extreme handed governance of StackStorm to the Linux Foundation, reporting about 1,200 installations a month and over 400 contributors. Extreme then contributed Workflow Composer’s enterprise code, including RBAC, LDAP and single sign-on, which reached the open-source releases in 2020 and 2021. Since then a technical steering committee of volunteers from user companies has kept it going, with releases growing further apart.

choices.choice: Sensors, triggers, rules and actions as separate pieces
choices.why: Splitting “what happened” from “what to do” lets one alert start several automations and one action serve many rules, much as IFTTT links triggers to actions.

choices.choice: Any script can be an action
choices.why: Operations teams already had shell, Python and PowerShell runbooks; wrapping them in a metadata file made them callable, auditable and reusable without a rewrite.

StackStorm first used OpenStack’s Mistral, which needed its own database and authentication. Orquesta, released in beta in 2018, runs natively inside StackStorm, and Mistral was removed in 3.3 in October 2020.
Running fixes from Slack puts the command and its output in the channel where the team is talking, while still going through StackStorm’s permissions and audit.

timeline.text: StackStorm founded by Evan Powell and Dmitri Zimine
Leaves stealth in May and releases the platform as open source
Moves to Extreme Networks with Brocade’s data-centre business
Orquesta workflow engine released in beta (2.8)
Extreme hands StackStorm to the Linux Foundation on 7 October
Mistral removed in 3.3; Orquesta is the only workflow engine
3.9.0 in October adds Python 3.10 and 3.11 and MongoDB 7.0
